explanations.explanation: That's the verdict, friend. The priest sees two things at once: the hair in the spot has turned white, and the sore appears deeper than the skin. Verse 3 says, “…it is a skin disease. After the priest examines him, he must pronounce him unclean.” I don't pull a batch out of the oven on a hunch either. I look first, and so does the priest.

explanations.answer: He shaves the spot and waits
explanations.explanation: Shaving does come up in this chapter, but later, for a scaly outbreak (Leviticus 13:33). Here the priest sees white hair and a sore that appears to be deeper than the skin. Verse 3 says that in this case, “…it is a skin disease.” So he pronounces the person unclean instead of waiting. Seven days apart is for when the spot doesn't appear deeper and the hair hasn't turned white (Leviticus 13:4).

explanations.answer: He sends the person to wash in the river
explanations.explanation: A river trip? Nobody here is packing swim trunks, friend. Washing does come up in this chapter, but it's clothes (Leviticus 13:6, 34) or a mildewed article (Leviticus 13:54). None of it is the answer to this verdict. In verse 3 the priest examines the person and “…must pronounce him unclean.”

Seven it is. Verse 4 says the priest “…shall isolate the infected person for seven days.” That's the in-between answer for a spot that isn't clearly a disease yet. It's a week of letting the spot show what it really is.
Three days would be a quick wait, but the text gives a different number. It says seven days for the maybe. Three would barely give a spot time to get comfortable.
Forty days would be a LONG time to stare at one spot. The text says seven for this maybe. Forty would be a whole new level of patience, and I don't think anybody signed up for that.

I see why it feels that way, since nothing changed and nothing spread. But verse 5 says the priest “…must isolate him for another seven days.” Staying the same isn't being pronounced clean yet. The text gives another week, and it doesn't say where the person spends it.

Right, not clean yet. Verse 5 says that if the infection is unchanged and hasn't spread, “…the priest must isolate him for another seven days.” A second week, then the priest examines again (Leviticus 13:6). The ruling comes after that.

Clean is the word. Verse 6 says that if the sore has faded and hasn't spread, “…the priest shall pronounce him clean; it is a rash.” The person must also wash his clothes and be clean. That's where the two weeks of waiting end.

Unclean is the ruling when the rash has spread (Leviticus 13:8). Here the sore has faded and has not spread. Verse 6 says in that case, “…the priest shall pronounce him clean; it is a rash.” So this one goes the other way.

Diseased isn't the word the priest uses here. When the sore has faded and has not spread, verse 6 says he “…shall pronounce him clean; it is a rash.” Skin disease is what he says when the rash has spread (Leviticus 13:8). So clean is the ruling in this case.
Clothes is right. Verse 6 says, “The person must wash his clothes and be clean.” It's a laundry day with good news attached. I'd gladly do that wash.
Hands make sense, since that's the first thing most of us would wash. But verse 6 names something else. It says the person “…must wash his clothes…” The text doesn't mention hands here.
Feet aren't mentioned in this verse. The text says the person must wash his clothes, and then he is clean (Leviticus 13:6). Easy to wander off on that one.

Yes. Verse 8 says, “…the priest must pronounce him unclean; it is a skin disease.” The spread is what changes the answer, because the rash was clean after the first two weeks only while it stayed put. Once it moves, the verdict moves with it.

Scar is a word the chapter uses elsewhere, for a spot after a boil or a burn that is unchanged and hasn't spread (Leviticus 13:23, 28). This rash has spread, though. Verse 8 says, “…it is a skin disease.” So the priest doesn't call it a scar.

The priest never calls it a bump. When the rash has spread, verse 8 says he “…must pronounce him unclean; it is a skin disease.” The spreading is what matters. Calling it a bump would be the optimist's answer, and I love an optimist.

Yes. Verse 11 says, “…it is a chronic skin disease and the priest must pronounce him unclean.” Then it adds, “He need not isolate him, for he is unclean.” No maybe week here. When the signs are this plain, the priest says so right away.

It's true, and the detail is in verse 11. The priest “…must pronounce him unclean.” and the text says, “He need not isolate him, for he is unclean.” The waiting week is for the maybe cases. This one isn't a maybe.

I know. I did a double take too. Verse 13 says, “Since it has all turned white, he is clean.” The disease covering the whole body, all turned white, is what makes the priest pronounce clean. Then verse 14 adds that raw flesh makes someone unclean.

That's the natural guess, since head to foot sounds like the worst case. But verse 13 says that when the disease has covered the entire body, the priest “…is to pronounce the infected person clean.” The reason is given right there: “Since it has all turned white, he is clean.” Nothing about this chapter is what I'd have guessed.

explanations.answer: The person must wait a week
explanations.explanation: Waiting a week is for the maybe cases, when a spot isn't clear yet. Here the priest doesn't wait. Verse 13 says that when it has all turned white, he “…is to pronounce the infected person clean.” The answer comes at once.

Yes. Verse 17 says, “…if the infection has turned white, the priest is to pronounce the infected person clean; then he is clean.” White is the same word that made the head-to-foot case clean. The raw flesh was unclean (Leviticus 13:15), but once it turns white, the answer changes.

I see why you'd lean that way. The raw flesh was called unclean back in verse 15. But verse 16 says if the raw flesh turns white, he goes to the priest, and verse 17 says the priest is to pronounce him clean. The turn to white changes the ruling.

explanations.answer: The person must leave the camp
explanations.explanation: Leaving the camp isn't mentioned in this case. Verse 17 says the priest is to pronounce the person clean. Living alone outside the camp comes up later for someone who has the infection (Leviticus 13:46). This person's infection turned white, so no leaving.

explanations.answer: White hair and beneath the skin
explanations.explanation: Yes. Verse 20 says, “…if it appears to be beneath the skin and the hair in it has turned white, the priest shall pronounce him unclean…” Same two signs we saw at the very start of the chapter. The priest is looking for the same pair.

explanations.answer: Black hair and a faded spot
explanations.explanation: Those two don't make the priest say unclean. Seven days apart is for a spot with no white hair in it, not beneath the skin, and faded (Leviticus 13:21). Black hair comes up later, when a scaly outbreak is unchanged and black hair has grown in it (Leviticus 13:37). So this pair isn't the unclean signs.

explanations.answer: Gray hair and a dry spot
explanations.explanation: Gray hair and dry spots don't appear anywhere in this chapter's list. The two signs in verse 20 are white hair and a spot beneath the skin. The choices were colorful, but the text sticks to white.

Scar is the word. Verse 23 says, “…it is only the scar from the boil, and the priest shall pronounce him clean.” A spot that stays the same and doesn't spread is only left over from the boil. It's a reminder, not a problem.

Blister is a reasonable guess, but it's not the word in the text. Verse 23 says the spot is “…only the scar from the boil…” That's what the unchanged spot turns out to be, and the person is pronounced clean.
The text doesn't use bruise here. Verse 23 says the spot that stays the same is “…only the scar from the boil…” After that, the priest pronounces the person clean.

Yellow and thin is the sign. Verse 30 says, “…if it appears to be deeper than the skin and the hair in it is yellow and thin, the priest must pronounce him unclean…” The text calls it “…a scaly outbreak…” Every spot has its own sign, and this one is hair that's yellow and thin.

Black hair points the other way in this part of the chapter. Verse 31 says the maybe case is when there's “…no black hair in it…” And black hair growing in an unchanged outbreak means it has healed (Leviticus 13:37). The unclean sign here is yellow and thin.
Gray and curly doesn't appear in the text. The sign for the head or chin is hair that is “…yellow and thin…” (Leviticus 13:30). That's the one the priest watches for.

explanations.answer: Shave except for the scaly area
explanations.explanation: Yes. Verse 33 says, “…the person must shave himself except for the scaly area.” Then the priest isolates him for another seven days. On the seventh day, the priest examines the scaly outbreak again (Leviticus 13:34).

explanations.answer: Cover the area with a cloth
explanations.explanation: A cloth sounds sensible, like a tea towel over a cooling rack. But that's not the step in verse 33. There the person “…must shave himself except for the scaly area.” Then the priest isolates him for another seven days.

explanations.answer: Wash the area in running water
explanations.explanation: Washing comes later, and it's for clothes once the person is pronounced clean (Leviticus 13:34). Before the second week, the text says the person “…must shave himself except for the scaly area.” Nothing about running water.

I get why you'd think so, since the yellow hair was the sign earlier. But verse 36 says, “…the priest need not look for yellow hair; the person is unclean.” Once it spreads after the cleansing, the spreading itself is enough.

Right. Verse 36 says that if the outbreak has spread, “…the priest need not look for yellow hair; the person is unclean.” The yellow hair mattered earlier, but once the outbreak spreads, there's no need to look. Spreading settles it.

Healed is right. Verse 37 says that if the outbreak is unchanged and black hair has grown in it, “…then it has healed. He is clean…” Black hair is the good sign here. Yellow hair meant trouble, so black hair is the opposite.
Chronic disease is a different case, the white swelling with raw flesh (Leviticus 13:10-11). Here the outbreak is unchanged and black hair has grown in. Verse 37 says, “…then it has healed.”

No more waiting here. Verse 37 says the outbreak is unchanged and black hair has grown in it, so “…it has healed.” The priest is to pronounce the person clean. The waiting weeks were for the maybe cases.

Harmless is the word, and it's good news. Verse 39 says, “…if the spots are dull white, it is a harmless rash that has broken out on the skin; the person is clean.” The priest looks, the spots are dull white, and the person is clean. I do a happy dance right here on my gold base. Dull white spots, harmless rash, clean.
Chronic is the word for the white swelling with raw flesh (Leviticus 13:11). Dull white spots are a different case. Verse 39 calls them “…a harmless rash…” and the person is clean.
Scaly is the word for the outbreak on the head or chin (Leviticus 13:30). These are white spots on the skin. If they're dull white, verse 39 calls them “…a harmless rash…”
Not quite, friend. Verse 40 says, “Now if a man loses his hair and is bald, he is still clean.” Verse 41 says the same for a receding hairline. Losing hair doesn't make anyone unclean.

Right. Verse 40 says, “Now if a man loses his hair and is bald, he is still clean.” Verse 41 says a receding hairline is the same. The trouble comes only if there's a reddish-white sore on the bald head or forehead (Leviticus 13:42).

Mouth is right. Verse 45 says the person “…must cover his mouth and cry out, ‘Unclean, unclean!’” I think this is one of the heavy parts of the chapter. It's a hard way to live, and it's good to read it plainly.
Eyes aren't mentioned. Verse 45 says the person “…must cover his mouth and cry out, ‘Unclean, unclean!’” I think this part of the chapter is heavy, so it's worth getting the detail right.

Hands aren't mentioned in this verse. The text says the person must wear torn clothes, let his hair hang loose, and “…cover his mouth and cry out, ‘Unclean, unclean!’” I think it's a heavy verse, and the mouth is the detail it gives.

Yes. Verse 46 says, “As long as he has the infection, he remains unclean. He must live alone in a place outside the camp.” That is the place the text gives for a person who has the infection. I think this one hurts to read.
The text doesn't put the person there. Verse 46 says, “He must live alone in a place outside the camp.” The Tent of Meeting isn't mentioned in that verse. The words are alone, and outside the camp.

No, the text says something else. Verse 46 says the person “…must live alone in a place outside the camp.” The priests' families aren't mentioned in that verse. Alone and outside the camp is what it says.

Green is one of the two. Verse 49 says, “…if the mark in the fabric, leather, weave, knit, or leather article is green or red, then it is contaminated with mildew and must be shown to the priest.” So a green mark means a trip to the priest.
Red is the other half. Verse 49 says the mark is “…green or red…” and then the item “…must be shown to the priest.” Green and red together are the pair. Neither one gets a pass.
Blue isn't in the text. Verse 49 names two colors for the mark, green and red. Blue would have been a nice surprise, but no.
Black isn't named for the mark on fabric. Black hair showed up earlier in the skin laws (Leviticus 13:37), but verse 49 says the mildew mark is green or red. Different color, different case.
White was the color of the skin signs earlier in the chapter. For fabric and leather, verse 49 gives two colors, green and red. White doesn't make the list for mildew.
Yes. Verse 50 says, “…the priest is to examine the mildew and isolate the contaminated fabric for seven days.” Same as the maybe cases on the skin. The item gets its own seven-day wait.

Burning does come up, but not first. Verse 50 says the priest isolates the item for seven days. Only if the mildew has spread on day seven does verse 52 say it's burned. The wait comes before the fire.

explanations.answer: Hand it back to the owner
explanations.explanation: The text says the priest isolates the item. Verse 50 says he is to “…isolate the contaminated fabric for seven days.” Handing it back isn't a step in the text. Seven days of isolation come first, then he examines it again (Leviticus 13:51).
Yes. Verse 52 says, “Since the mildew is harmful, the article must be burned up.” That covers wool, linen or leather. Once the mildew has spread, the item is done.

explanations.answer: It is buried outside the camp
explanations.explanation: Burying isn't in the text. Verse 52 says, “…the article must be burned up.” Outside the camp comes up for a person with the infection (Leviticus 13:46), not for this item.

explanations.answer: It is kept by the priest
explanations.explanation: The priest isolates the item during the seven days (Leviticus 13:50), but that isn't how it ends. Once the mildew has spread, verse 52 says, “…the article must be burned up.” Keeping it isn't the instruction.

It's an understandable guess, but the text says otherwise. Verse 55 says that if the mildewed article hasn't changed in appearance after washing, “…it is unclean. Even though the mildew has not spread, you must burn it…” Not spreading doesn't save it.

Right. Verse 55 says, “Even though the mildew has not spread, you must burn it, whether the rot is on the front or back.” The washing didn't change how it looks, so the item is unclean. Not spreading isn't enough here.

BURN IT, baker! Verse 57 says, “But if it reappears in the fabric, weave, or knit, or on any leather article, it is spreading. You must burn the contaminated article.” The priest already tried cutting out the mildewed section in verse 56. When the mildew comes back, the text doesn't send him for a second snip. It says burn.
The text doesn't give a second cutting. Verse 57 says that if it reappears, “…it is spreading. You must burn the contaminated article.” The snip only works once.
Sun isn't mentioned in this passage. For mildew that comes back, verse 57 says, “You must burn the contaminated article.” That's the instruction, with no sunbathing step.

Yes. Verse 58 says, “If the mildew disappears from the fabric, weave, or knit, or any leather article after washing, then it is to be washed again, and it will be clean.” One more wash and the item is clean. A happy ending for a piece of laundry.
It's true, and verse 58 says so. If the mildew disappears after washing, “…then it is to be washed again, and it will be clean.” So there's one more wash, and then the item is clean.
